At least 38 Yemeni troops killed in Houthi attacks
item.description:
Houthi missile and drone attacks in Yemen on Thursday killed at least 38 government troops and injured 29, two medical sources told AFP, in one of the deadliest days between the two sides in years.
A military official told AFP that a military camp in the al-Ruwaik area of Marib province, in central Yemen, had been attacked, as well as camps in the Al-Abr and Al-Wadiah areas of Hadramawt, near the border with Saudi Arabia.
One of the missile attacks hit troops during their morning formation at the camp in Marib province, “killing and wounding at least 45 personnel,” said another military source, who declined to be named for security reasons.
Yemen, which has been embroiled in more than a decade of war, last month became the latest front to be sucked into the US-Iran war, as the Tehran-backed Houthi rebels upended a 2022 truce with the Saudi-backed government.
The rebels welcomed an Iranian plane directly in the capital Sanaa, triggering tit-for-tat attacks, and they later announced a maritime blockade of the kingdom and began hitting its tankers.
Last month, the Houthis killed 16 troops in an attack on government-aligned forces south of the port city of Hodeidah, two medical officials told AFP.
The Houthis have been at war with the government since 2014 in a conflict that has killed hundreds of thousands of people and triggered a major humanitarian crisis in Yemen.
The rebels control Yemen’s capital Sanaa and much of the populous north, while the internationally recognized government holds much of the south.
The fighting between the two sides has largely been frozen since a UN-negotiated truce in 2022 that had held despite expiring.

item.title: To Civilization
item.description: Give back the forest, take this city away in return, Take your iron, brick, timber and stone O new civilization, O ruthless devourer, Give back the hermit’s grove and its sacred cover, Those untainted days, the bathing at dusk, The grazing herds, the quiet Sama chant, The fistful of wild rice, the bark cloth, Immersing within the self, discussing day after day The Great Truths. In your stone cage I refuse to have your royal feast kept safe. I want to break free and spread my wings, I want my own strength back within me, I want to tear the bonds apart to let the heartbeat of the universe touch my soul.

item.title: Iran threatened to ‘black out’ Gulf if US hit power plants
item.description:
Iran intensified its threats towards its Gulf neighbors last week, conveying messages that it would “black out” the entire region if the United States struck its power plants and rattling off a list of specific targets, two officials told AFP.
The warning followed threats by US President Donald Trump of a massive attack against Iran, which he later walked back over the weekend citing requests from Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Qatar and hope for a breakthrough in talks.
“Iran threatened to black out the Gulf, country by country, if Trump attacked its power plants,” a Gulf official told AFP, with another regional official confirming the messaging.
Both spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive matters.
Trump said the planned strikes would have been “the biggest attack since World War II,” with US media reporting he was considering hitting energy infrastructure, as he has repeatedly threatened to do.
Iran conveyed through intermediaries that any attacks on its power plants would trigger strikes on the same targets in the Gulf, the officials said.
It had publicly made such threats before, but the new one was “very serious,” the Gulf official said, noting it included “a long list of targets they would attack.”
In mid-July, Trump threatened to destroy an Iranian bridge or power plant for every attack on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran warning of an “eye for an eye” response.
The Gulf official said Iran’s message said it would hit power plants and water desalination facilities, which the mostly desert region largely relies on for drinking water.
After Trump called off the strikes, Saudi Arabia announced that Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman had spoken to the US leader in a call aimed at reducing regional tensions.
The Gulf has borne the brunt of Iran’s attacks during the Middle East war, with strikes targeting US assets as well as civilian infrastructure such as energy sites, ports and airports.
Sporadic attacks continued after a ceasefire and subsequent memorandum of understanding were agreed in April and June, respectively.
But the exchanges of fire increased in scale and regularity as the ceasefire fell apart in July, with strikes targeting mainly Kuwait and Bahrain.

item.title: Why Bangladesh must rediscover the joy of reading
item.description:
A few weeks ago, I attended an extempore storytelling session at Pabna Square School & College, where I had the privilege of serving as the lead storyteller.
One by one, ten students stepped forward to continue the story, each adding unexpected twists, suspense and imaginative endings.
Their confidence and creativity were remarkable, reminding me that children do not need to be taught curiosity -- they simply need opportunities to express it.
The school itself reflected that philosophy.
What impressed me most was not only the enthusiasm of the students but also the institution’s thoughtfully designed environment, including two separate libraries -- one for school students and another for college learners.
It was a quiet reminder that a library is more than a room filled with books. It is a place where imagination begins.
Reading remains one of the most valuable habits a child can develop.
It nurtures creativity, broadens knowledge, strengthens critical thinking and builds confidence.
Books introduce young minds to different cultures, ideas and perspectives while fostering empathy and curiosity.
Yet despite living in an age where information is more accessible than ever, reading for pleasure is steadily losing ground to screens.
Walk into many classrooms across Bangladesh today and you will find students who can recite textbook chapters from memory but rarely read beyond the prescribed syllabus.
Those who do are often encouraged -- sometimes by well-meaning parents -- to return to guidebooks, coaching notes and examination preparation. Storybooks, novels and general reading are frequently treated as distractions rather than essential parts of a child’s intellectual development.
This reflects a broader problem within our education system.
An examination-driven culture rewards memorisation over understanding, while classroom teaching often prioritises completing the syllabus instead of encouraging curiosity.
Socio-economic realities also play a role.
For many families, examination results are viewed as the safest route to higher education, employment and financial security. As a result, reading beyond the syllabus is often seen as a luxury rather than an investment.
A newer challenge has emerged in recent years. Smartphones, social media and increasingly AI-powered tools now offer instant answers without requiring sustained engagement with books.
While these technologies are valuable when used responsibly, they can also discourage deep reading and independent thinking. When students rely on quick summaries instead of reading complete texts, they miss the intellectual discipline, imagination and analytical skills that long-form reading develops.
This should not be mistaken for a lack of curiosity among young people. Rather, it is the predictable outcome of a system that places examinations at the centre of learning.
If Bangladesh wants to cultivate confident, independent thinkers, reading must become more than an extracurricular activity, it must become an integral part of education.
Reading and storytelling are inseparable. Schools often ask students to read stories from textbooks, yet rarely encourage them to tell stories of their own or learn how stories are created. Children have an innate love for storytelling. Stories spark imagination, create wonder and help young people understand themselves and others. They expose readers to different cultures and perspectives while nurturing empathy, tolerance and respect.
Research consistently shows that children who read regularly outside the classroom perform better across subjects. Reading strengthens concentration, expands vocabulary, improves communication skills and develops critical thinking. More importantly, it teaches emotional intelligence. Through fictional characters, children learn to recognise feelings such as grief, anger, jealousy and hope, discovering healthy ways to navigate their own emotions.
These qualities are increasingly valuable in a world where creativity and problem-solving matter as much as academic credentials. A workforce capable of innovation cannot be built on rote memorisation alone.
Several barriers continue to hinder the growth of a reading culture in Bangladesh. Access to quality education remains deeply unequal. Urban centres generally offer better-resourced schools, while many rural institutions—particularly in haor, char and hill-tract areas—continue to struggle with inadequate infrastructure, teacher shortages and overcrowded classrooms. Even where school libraries exist, they are often poorly stocked, inaccessible or treated as storage rooms instead of active learning spaces.
The examination-oriented education system leaves little incentive for teachers, parents or students to prioritise reading beyond the curriculum. At the same time, smartphones and social media increasingly compete for children’s attention, replacing the time that earlier generations devoted to books.
Changing this culture requires action at multiple levels.
Every primary and secondary school, madrasa and educational institution should have a functioning library. These should not be silent, dusty rooms visited only occasionally, but welcoming spaces with comfortable seating, colourful displays and regular storytelling sessions that encourage children to develop a lifelong relationship with books. Even schools with limited resources can begin with modest reading corners created from donated books while working towards larger library collections.
Reading should also become a shared social activity. Book clubs, reading circles and read-aloud sessions allow students to exchange ideas and discover that books are meant to be discussed as much as they are read. A weekly reading period, free from textbooks and examinations, could help students develop the habit of reading simply for enjoyment.
Teachers play an equally important role. A teacher who speaks passionately about a favourite novel often inspires students far more effectively than repeated lectures about the importance of reading. Educators should be encouraged to recommend books, discuss literature and integrate wider reading into classroom activities.
Technology, often viewed as the enemy of reading, can also become an ally. Audiobooks, digital libraries and reading applications can make books more accessible, particularly for students who lack nearby libraries or cannot afford to buy books. Used wisely, digital platforms can expand rather than diminish reading opportunities.
Schools can further encourage reading through book review competitions, reading challenges and recognition programs that celebrate students’ reading habits alongside their academic achievements.
Bangladesh already has organisations demonstrating what is possible. Jatio Grantho Kendro has long promoted reading through affordable books and community library initiatives. Bishwo Sahitto Kendro’s mobile library service continues to bring books directly to neighbourhoods across the country. Storytelling initiatives such as GOLPOKAR help nurture children’s imagination, creativity and language skills by encouraging them to engage with stories beyond the classroom.
Annual book fairs also offer valuable opportunities to cultivate young readers. Schools should organise visits that allow students to browse books across different genres, meet authors and experience the excitement of a community united by reading.
Transforming Bangladesh’s reading culture will not happen overnight, nor can it be achieved by any single institution. It requires schools that value curiosity, teachers who inspire reading, families that encourage it, publishers who make books accessible and policymakers who recognise reading as a national investment.
The students I met in Pabna reminded me that the desire to imagine, create and tell stories is already there. What they, and millions of children across Bangladesh, need is an environment that nurtures that curiosity rather than confines it to examination halls.
If we want future generations to become thoughtful citizens, creative professionals and compassionate leaders, we must first help them become readers. Investing in reading today is ultimately an investment in the Bangladesh of tomorrow.

item.title: PM to hand over new houses to 100 flood-affected families in Banshkhali
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is set to deliver new homes to 100 families who were rendered homeless by the recent devastating floods in the Banshkhali upazila of the district. The prime minister will hand over the keys of these homes to the affected families during a rally in Banshkhali on Sunday as part of his visit to Cox's Bazar and Chittagong, said Mohammad Sharif Uddin, additional deputy commissioner (General), Chittagong.
"The families who lost everything to the floodwaters found themselves in a dire situation, and the government's initiative to provide them with housing has instilled a renewed sense of hope. They are filled with joy that the government is reconstructing homes on their own land, and that Prime Minister Tarique Rahman will personally hand over the keys. They are eagerly anticipating the opportunity to meet the prime minister and receive the keys of their new homes," he added.
As per sources from the district administration, a total of 100 affected families have been identified, with 10 families each in Banshkhali Municipality and nine unions. The reconstruction of their homes is being funded by the government. In consideration of natural disasters, particularly floods, the construction of these houses incorporates RCC pillars, wood, and tin.
The design of the houses is deemed "disaster-tolerant" due to the use of tin for enclosure and roofing. Each tin house measures 18 feet in length and 12 feet in width, comprising two rooms.
Additionally, there will be an attached toilet measuring five feet by five feet. Former mayor of Banshkhali Municipality, Kamrul Islam Hossaini, said: “Families whose homes were destroyed by the flood and who lack the means to construct new houses have been identified to receive housing from the Prime Minister.”
Talking to BSS, Additional Deputy Commissioner (General) of Chittagong Mohammad Sharif Uddin said: “The Honorable prime minister is scheduled to visit three upazilas in Chittagong next Sunday. Among these, 100 families affected by the recent floods in Banshkhali will receive the keys to their new homes. The construction of these houses is nearing completion, funded by the local government department.”
Meanwhile, Chittagong Deputy Commissioner Mohammad Zahidul Islam Mian, conducted an inspection of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s forthcoming visit to Banshkhali and the ongoing construction of houses for flood-affected families. He toured the site and the houses being built near Baharchhara beach in Banshkhali upazila. Preparations are in full swing at the designated venue adjacent to Baharchhara beach ahead of the prime minister’s visit. The deputy commissioner reviewed the construction of the stage and pandal, security measures, seating arrangements for guests, and the overall management of the venue. He engaged with the officials responsible and relevant parties regarding the progress of the preparations. Chittagong Deputy Commissioner Mohammad Zahidul Islam Mian told BSS that the overall arrangements for the prime minister's visit are advancing swiftly. “I have inspected the venue in Baharchhara, Banshkhali, and have instructed all involved to remain vigilant in every aspect to ensure the event is organized smoothly,” he added. Concerning the provision of housing for the affected individuals, the deputy commissioner remarked: “I have communicated with the engineers and construction workers regarding the structural integrity and quality of the work being done on the houses.”

item.title: Before Stockholm, there was Shilaidaha
item.description:
Before Rabindranath Tagore became a Nobel laureate, he was a landlord who spent long afternoons on a boat on the Padma, in what is now Kushtia.
Tagore took charge of managing his family’s zamindari estate at Shilaidaha in 1890, arriving there for the first time that November and returning at intervals throughout the following decade. He worked and wrote between a three-storeyed house on the riverbank and a houseboat on the Padma. According to the historical records of Shilaidaha Rabindra Kuthibari, it was during a stay there in 1912 that Tagore began translating the poems that would become Gitanjali into English—the same manuscript he carried with him when he sailed for London later that year. The house still stands, preserved by Bangladesh’s Department of Archaeology, and continues to draw visitors on his birth and death anniversaries.
The London chapter of the story is better known, though it is often simplified. Tagore’s son, Rathindranath, had the translated notebook in his keeping and accidentally left it behind on a train. In his memoirs, he recalled rushing to the Underground’s lost-property office to recover it, later wondering how differently events might have unfolded had the manuscript been lost forever. Once it was safely back in hand, Tagore showed the translations to the painter William Rothenstein, who arranged a private reading on July 7, 1912 for a small circle of literary figures, including W.B. Yeats. Deeply impressed, Yeats agreed to write the introduction. Gitanjali: Song Offerings was published that November.
A year later, the Nobel Committee in Stockholm announced its decision. The citation, preserved on the Nobel Foundation’s website, praised Tagore’s verse as “profoundly sensitive, fresh and beautiful.” He became the first Asian recipient of the Nobel Prize in Literature—an honour based, it is worth remembering, on a single volume of English translations that represented only a small part of a literary output spanning more than fifty volumes of poetry, most of which remained unavailable in English.
International recognition transformed Tagore’s reputation, but not his priorities. More than a decade earlier, on a stretch of land near Bolpur that his father had set aside as a place of spiritual retreat, Tagore had already begun pursuing another ambition. In December 1901, he opened a school there with just five students, holding classes beneath the open sky in deliberate contrast to the rigid, classroom-bound education he himself had disliked. That school became Santiniketan.
By 1921, it had grown into Visva-Bharati University, conceived as a meeting ground where Eastern and Western scholarship could engage on equal terms at a time when nationalist sentiment across both Europe and the Indian subcontinent was becoming increasingly rigid. Through the Visva-Bharati Act of 1951, India’s Parliament declared it a central university and an institution of national importance. More than 120 years after it began beneath a handful of trees, Unesco inscribed Santiniketan on its World Heritage List in September 2023.
Tagore’s work on his family’s rural estates was far more than an interruption to his literary life, and it extended well beyond Shilaidaha. At Patisar, another family estate in what is now Naogaon district, he was effectively pioneering rural development decades before the term existed. Farmers along the Atrai River were routinely devastated by seasonal floods and trapped by the crippling interest rates of local moneylenders. In response, Tagore established a credit scheme that historians studying the estate today regard as one of the region’s earliest experiments in microcredit. Estate records show that he visited Patisar at least fourteen times between 1891 and 1937, dividing his days between poetry and the practical demands of managing a working estate.
It is a chapter of Tagore’s life that rarely appears in accounts written outside Bangladesh: the country that would one day become synonymous with microfinance had, more than a century earlier, witnessed an early experiment in the same idea under the stewardship of the poet who would eventually write its national anthem.
The story of that anthem begins not with patriotism, but with protest. In 1905, the British colonial administration partitioned Bengal along religious lines, calculating that a divided province would be easier to govern than a united one. Tagore was outraged. He responded by writing Amar Sonar Bangla, setting its words to a melody he associated with Gagan Harkara, the postman and Baul singer whose songs had long stayed with him. It was a lament for a Bengal Tagore hoped would one day be reunited. The partition was eventually reversed in 1911, though not in the way its opponents had originally envisioned.
Six years after writing Amar Sonar Bangla, Tagore composed another song for an entirely different occasion—a session of the Indian National Congress in Calcutta in December 1911. His niece, Indira Devi, hurriedly transcribed the notation as he hummed the melody, allowing it to be performed within days of its composition. In 1950, independent India adopted a shortened version of that song, Jana Gana Mana, as its national anthem. Twenty-one years later, during Bangladesh’s Liberation War, the opening lines of Amar Sonar Bangla—the protest song written against Bengal’s partition decades earlier—became the national anthem of Bangladesh.
Neither composition was written with the expectation that it would one day become a national symbol. Yet, on two separate occasions, roughly four decades apart, one poet composed the anthems of two nations that did not yet exist at the time he wrote them—a distinction that, as far as historians have established, belongs to no other writer.
The next major turn in Tagore’s creative life began aboard a ship. In 1924, while travelling to Peru, he fell ill and was forced to disembark in Buenos Aires. There, the Argentine writer Victoria Ocampo welcomed him to recover at her family’s estate in San Isidro. During his convalescence, Ocampo noticed the curious drawings filling the margins of Tagore’s manuscript of Purabi—forms that had gradually emerged from the words he had crossed out while revising his poems. Intrigued by what she saw, she wrote to Georges-Henri Rivière, curator of the Trocadéro Museum in Paris, urging him to organise an exhibition. The result was a landmark exhibition at the Galerie Pigalle, which opened on May 2, 1930, displaying around 400 of Tagore’s paintings alongside African and Oceanic art.
Tagore himself remained remarkably unsentimental about his paintings. In a letter to William Rothenstein, he wrote that they possessed “psychological interest” largely because they were the products of “untutored fingers and an untrained mind.” He was already past sixty when he began painting in earnest and had never received any formal artistic training. Yet by the time of his death, he had created more than two thousand works, dense ink-and-wash compositions that many art historians now place closer to European modernism than to anything else being produced in India at the time.
Tagore died on August 6, 1941 at Jorasanko, the same Calcutta house where he had been born eighty years earlier. Looking back, it is easy to see a Nobel laureate, an educator, a rural reformer, a songwriter and a painter, as though they were all part of a carefully designed life’s work. They were not. Tagore simply kept following his curiosity—from a houseboat on the Padma to a school beneath the trees of Santiniketan, from village credit schemes to Nobel-winning poetry, from national anthems to paintings that emerged almost by accident from the margins of his manuscripts. That may be the most remarkable thing about him: not that he mastered so many fields, but that he never allowed himself to be confined to just one.

Where to begin with Rabindranath Tagore on screen
item.description:
Eighty-five years after Rabindranath Tagore’s passing, his stories continue to shape cinema in ways few writers ever have.
From Satyajit Ray’s intimate literary adaptations to modern reinterpretations, generations of filmmakers across Bangla and Hindi cinema have returned to Tagore’s fiction for its timeless exploration of love, loss, identity and human relationships.
On the 85th anniversary of the Nobel laureate’s death at his ancestral home in Jorasanko, here are eight essential films that reveal why his literary legacy remains so enduring on screen.
Made to commemorate Tagore’s birth centenary, Teen Kanya brings together three of his celebrated short stories—The Postmaster, Monihara and Samapti—into a remarkable anthology. It remains one of the finest introductions to Tagore’s fictional universe and a testament to Ray’s profound understanding of the writer’s emotional and philosophical depth.
Teen Kanya (1961) — Directed by Satyajit Ray. Photo: Wikipedia
Often regarded as Ray’s masterpiece—and the film he himself described as having “the fewest flaws”—Charulata adapts Tagore’s novella Nastanirh. Madhabi Mukherjee delivers an unforgettable performance as an intelligent, lonely woman trapped in an emotionally unfulfilling marriage, in what remains one of Indian cinema’s most nuanced portraits of desire and solitude.
Charulata (1964) — Directed by Satyajit Ray. Photo: Wikipedia
Ray’s final feature adapted from Tagore explores the collision between personal relationships and political ideology. Based on the celebrated novel, the film examines marriage, nationalism and identity during the Swadeshi movement, revealing the complexities that lie beneath patriotic fervour.
Ghare Baire (1984) — Directed by Satyajit Ray. Photo: Wikipedia
Perhaps Tagore’s most universally loved story, Kabuliwala follows an Afghan dry-fruit seller in Kolkata who develops a tender bond with a little girl who reminds him of his daughter back home. Chhabi Biswas delivers a deeply moving performance in a film that continues to define the emotional power of Tagore’s storytelling.
Kabuliwala (1957) — Directed by Tapan Sinha. Photo: Wikipedia
Hindi cinema’s adaptation brought Tagore’s beloved story to an even wider audience. Balraj Sahni reportedly lived among Afghan immigrants in Bombay to prepare for the role, while Manna Dey’s immortal rendition of Aye Mere Pyaare Watan remains one of Hindi cinema’s most poignant songs of exile and longing.
Kabuliwala (1961) — Directed by Hemen Gupta. Photo: Wikipedia
Though not a direct adaptation, Bimal Roy’s landmark classic draws inspiration from Tagore’s poem Dui Bigha Jomi. Chronicling a poor farmer’s struggle against exploitation, the film became a cornerstone of Indian social realism and paved the way for a new wave of humanist cinema.
Do Bigha Zamin (1953) — Directed by Bimal Roy. Photo: Wikipedia
Rituparno Ghosh’s elegant adaptation casts Aishwarya Rai as Binodini, a young widow who refuses to accept the restrictive role society assigns her. Bold in its portrayal of female desire and emotional complexity, the film earned both critical acclaim and international recognition, including a National Film Award and a Golden Leopard nomination at the Locarno Film Festival.
Chokher Bali (2003) — Directed by Rituparno Ghosh. Photo: Wikipedia
Rather than retelling Kabuliwala, Bioscopewala reimagines its emotional core for a contemporary audience. Transforming the Afghan fruit seller into a travelling film projectionist, the film demonstrates the enduring flexibility of Tagore’s storytelling and its ability to find new meaning in changing times.
Bioscopewala (2018) — Directed by Deb Medhekar. Photo: Wikipedia
More than eight decades after his death, Rabindranath Tagore remains one of Indian cinema’s most enduring literary inspirations. His stories continue to resonate because they speak not only to a particular place or period, but to the timeless complexities of the human condition.

item.title: Tonu murder: SC scraps bail of ex-Army member Hafizur
item.description:
The Appellate Division’s chamber court on Thursday stayed the High Court's order granting interim bail to former army member Hafizur Rahman, an accused in the murder case of Comilla’s Sohagi Jahan Tonu, and ordered him to surrender within 24 hours.
If Hafizur fails to surrender within the stipulated time, police have been directed to arrest him, Attorney General Md Ruhul Quddus Kazal said after the hearing.
The order came after the state challenged the High Court's August 2 decision granting Hafizur six months' interim bail.
The High Court bench of Justice Zafar Ahmed and Justice Sathika Hossain had also issued a rule asking why he should not be granted permanent bail and directed the authorities concerned to respond within four weeks.
Following the High Court order, Hafizur was released from jail, prompting the state to move the Appellate Division seeking cancellation of the bail.
Deputy Attorney General Shiuli Khanam and Assistant Attorneys General Sabbir Hossain, Md Mizanur Rahman, Rezaul Karim and Mir Moniruzzaman represented the state, while lawyer Muslem Uddin Bhuiyan appeared for Hafizur.
Hafizur, 52, a former senior warrant officer of the Bangladesh Army, was arrested by the Police Bureau of Investigation (PBI) from his residence in Keraniganj on April 21 in connection with the high-profile murder case.
Tonu, a student and private tutor, went missing on the evening of March 20, 2016, after going to a house inside Comilla Cantonment for a tutoring session. Her body was later recovered from a bush near the cantonment's power house area.
The murder has remained under investigation for years, drawing widespread public attention. Hafizur's arrest earlier this year renewed focus on the long-running case.

item.title: RAB arrests two with rare Sterling submachine gun, foreign pistol in Rajbari raids
item.description:
Members of Rapid Action Battalion (RAB) arrested two alleged armed men and seized a rare foreign-made Sterling submachine gun, a foreign-made pistol and 34 rounds of live ammunition in separate raids in Rajbari's Sadar and Goalanda upazilas.
The arrested men were identified as Md Momin Molla and Hasan Ali Biswas. RAB said they have links to the banned Sarbahara Party's Manju-Jahangir group.
The arrests were made in separate operations conducted by members of RAB-10's CPC-3 Faridpur Camp on Wednesday evening and night, RAB-10 Commanding Officer Additional DIG Md Asaduzzaman told a press conference at the RAB Media Centre in Karwan Bazar on Thursday afternoon.
Company Commander of RAB's Faridpur Camp, Major Farhan Mahmud Moktada, was also present.
Briefing reporters, the Commanding Officer said, acting on a tip-off, its members conducted the first raid at Mahishkhola Mollabari area under Pachuria Union in Rajbari Sadar around 6:45 pm on Wednesday. Momin Molla was arrested during the operation.
RAB recovered a foreign-made Sterling submachine gun, two magazines, 28 rounds of live ammunition and two mobile phones from his possession.
Asaduzzaman said Momin Molla is a Saudi Arabia expatriate who returned to Bangladesh about a month ago and was scheduled to fly back to Saudi Arabia on August 13.
He added that the recovered Sterling submachine gun is an extremely rare type of firearm.
In another operation around 10:15 pm the same day, RAB arrested Hasan Ali Biswas near Jalil Member Bridge in Chhoto Bhakla Union under Goalanda upazila.
During the raid, RAB recovered a foreign-made pistol, one magazine, six rounds of live ammunition, several locally made weapons, four mobile phones and Tk 15,300 in cash from his possession.
The RAB-10 chief said preliminary interrogation revealed that both arrested men have links to the Sarbahara Party, while Hasan Ali Biswas is associated with the party's Manju-Jahangir group.
He said RAB's drive to arrest the group's leader, Manju-Jahangir, is continuing.
He also said local residents had been disturbed by the alleged criminal activities of the arrested men. RAB will seek remand of the accused to identify the source of the weapons, their use and other associates.
RAB said cases under the Arms Act are being filed against the two men with the respective police stations and legal action is underway.

item.title: 'UN withheld July uprising eyewitness identities over death penalty provision'
item.description:
The United Nations did not share the identities of eyewitnesses cited in its fact-finding report on the July 2024 Mass Uprising because Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal (ICT) Act still retains the death penalty, a prosecutor told the tribunal on Thursday.
Prosecutor Gazi Monawar Hossain Tamim made the disclosure while presenting arguments before International Crimes Tribunal-2 in a crimes against humanity case against seven leaders of the now-banned Awami League and its affiliated organizations, including Awami League General Secretary Obaidul Quader.
During the hearing, Monawar said armed activists of the Chhatra League and Awami League attacked protesters between July 14 and July 17, 2024, on the instructions of senior party leaders, adding that the incidents were documented in the UN's fact-finding report.
He said the report contains references for all witnesses but the UN had informed the prosecution that it would disclose the identities of eyewitnesses only if the death penalty was removed from Bangladesh's ICT law.
"As a result, we did not receive the UN's eyewitnesses," the prosecutor said, adding that the prosecution is instead producing its own eyewitnesses before the tribunal.
Following the fall of the Awami League government during the Jul uprising, the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) published a fact-finding report examining events between July 1 and August 15, 2024.
The report held senior leaders of the then-ruling Awami League responsible for atrocities and crimes against humanity committed during the period.
To prepare the report, the UN fact-finding mission conducted investigations in eight cities—Dhaka, Chittagong, Rangpur, Rajshahi, Khulna, Bogra, Sylhet and Gazipur.
It interviewed more than 230 victims and eyewitnesses, along with 36 government officials, members of the security forces and political figures familiar with the events.
Monawar told the tribunal that the UN withheld the identities of those eyewitnesses because the ICT Act still provides for capital punishment. The United Nations has consistently called for the abolition of the death penalty for all crimes.
Besides Obaidul Quader, the accused are Awami League Joint General Secretary AFM Bahauddin Nasim, former state minister for Information and Broadcasting Mohammad Ali Arafat, Jubo League Chairman Sheikh Fazle Shams Parash and General Secretary Mainul Hossain Khan, and Chhatra League President Saddam Hossain and General Secretary Sheikh Wali Asif.
All seven accused are currently absconding.

item.title: Defence adviser: Migration management now part of national security
item.description:
Prime Minister's Defence Adviser Brig Gen (retd) Dr AKM Shamsul Islam on Thursday said migration management has become an integral part of national security amid evolving global and geopolitical realities.
Speaking as the keynote speaker at a program titled Migration Governance as a National Security Instrument in Bangladesh at the Bangladesh University of Professionals (BUP) in Mirpur Cantonment, he said migration is no longer solely an issue of the economy, employment or the labor market.
"It is directly linked to a country's internal stability, border management, humanitarian protection and overall national security," he said.
Shamsul said the concept of national security has expanded beyond protecting territorial boundaries to include safe migration, legal employment opportunities, orderly cross-border movement, and safeguarding the rights and dignity of Bangladeshis living abroad.
He warned that failure to ensure safe, orderly and well-managed migration could create multidimensional challenges for domestic stability, border security and regional peace.
Highlighting the importance of remittances to the economy, he stressed the need to develop a skilled workforce, expand opportunities for safe and regular migration, and equip prospective migrants with adequate knowledge, training and protection.
He also called for stronger coordination among relevant institutions to combat irregular migration, fraud, human trafficking and transnational criminal networks.
Describing Bangladeshi expatriates as valuable contributors to both the national economy and the country's global image, the defence adviser said the state's capacity must be strengthened to protect their rights, security and dignity while providing support during times of crisis.
"A well-coordinated, humane and security-conscious migration system can accelerate Bangladesh's economic progress while reinforcing national security," he said.
He also called for a forward-looking migration policy that integrates the economic, humanitarian, social and security dimensions of migration, emphasizing the importance of policy-oriented research, reliable data, skilled human resources and coordinated institutional efforts.
During an interactive session, BUP students raised questions on migration policy, human trafficking, the safety of Bangladeshi expatriates, border management, regional geopolitics and national security. Responding to the queries, the defence adviser highlighted the growing strategic importance of migration governance in the changing global order.
The event was attended by BUP Vice-Chancellor Maj Gen Md Mahbub-Ul Alam, senior military and civil officials, deans, faculty members, researchers and students.
Concluding the program, the defence adviser praised BUP's contributions to education, research and national development, expressing hope that the university would continue to play an active role in policy research, national dialogue and promoting security awareness among young people.

item.title: Dr Zahid: Family card program to be launched officially on Aug 16
item.description:
Social Welfare Minister Prof Dr A Z M Zahid Hossain on Thursday said the government's Family Card program will be officially launched on August 16 under the 2026–27 fiscal year.
He said Prime Minister Tarique Rahman will inaugurate the program from ward no-8 of Latifabad union in Kishoreganj Sadar Upazila.
The minister said the government plans to bring 4.1 million beneficiaries under the program in its first phase. It is expected that this program will be expanded over the next four years to cover approximately 16 million families across the country.
The decisions were taken at a meeting of the Cabinet Committee on the Family Card program, chaired by Finance Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury at the Bangladesh Secretariat here.
Briefing the reporters after the meeting, Prof Dr Zahid Hossain outlined various aspects of the initiative.
He said the primary objective of the Family Card program is to ensure that government social protection benefits reach genuine beneficiaries while promoting transparency and accountability in the beneficiary selection process.
"No eligible person should be left out, and no ineligible person should be included in the beneficiary list," the minister said, adding that the government is giving the matter the highest priority.
To achieve this, beneficiary information will be updated and reviewed regularly. The database will be revised in line with changes in the socio-economic conditions of households. Families that rise above the poverty line will be removed from the list, while newly eligible households will be added accordingly.
The minister said the government intends to develop the Family Card into a dynamic social registry rather than maintaining it as a static database.
Regular updates based on real-life changes will help to ensure the inclusion of eligible beneficiaries and reduce opportunities for irregularities in social protection programs.
He also said strict verification procedures would be followed at the union level to prevent any errors or irregularities in the distribution process.
Beneficiary information will be verified through local administration, public representatives and relevant officials. Fresh investigations will also be conducted where complaints are received.
According to the minister, the government's goal is to establish an accurate, technology-driven and modern social protection system that reflects changes in people's living conditions through continuous updates to the beneficiary database.
He said the current fiscal year's budget includes a plan to cover 4.1 million beneficiaries under the Family Card program. Following an assessment of its effectiveness, the government aims to expand coverage to around 16 million families over the next four years.
Senior officials from the relevant ministries and divisions attended the Cabinet Committee meeting, where implementation strategies, beneficiary selection, data verification, database management and field-level monitoring of the Family Card programme were discussed in detail.

Govt doctor faces dismissal for private practice during office hours
item.description:
A government doctor is set to face dismissal from service and cancellation of his medical licence after Health Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Hossain found him allegedly treating patients at a private diagnostic center during official working hours on Thursday.
The doctor, Dr Moinul Hasan Chishti, is posted at Belabo Upazila Health Complex in Narsingdi.
The minister found him during a surprise inspection at Popular Diagnostic Centre on English Road in Old Dhaka and immediately instructed the authorities concerned to revoke his medical licence and dismiss him from government service.
Speaking after the inspection, Sakhawat said government doctors are prohibited from providing medical services at private healthcare facilities during official office hours.
Alleging that Dr Chishti had been violating the rules for a long time, the minister said the doctor's office had previously served him with a show-cause notice, which he allegedly ignored.
"The doctor's office had also served him a show-cause notice, but he ignored it," the minister said.
He also directed the executive magistrate conducting the mobile court to take necessary legal action over the incident.
During the inspection, officials reviewed the clinic's records and found that it did not possess a resignation letter or a no-objection certificate (NOC) indicating that the doctor had resigned from government service or obtained permission to work at a private healthcare facility.
The minister also reprimanded the manager of Popular Diagnostic Centre for allowing a government physician to treat patients without verifying the required documents.
"If a government doctor wants to resign or work elsewhere, a resignation letter and NOC are mandatory. Allowing such practice without verifying these documents is illegal," he said, alleging that the clinic had facilitated unethical practices for financial gain.
The clinic manager acknowledged the lapse, admitting that the authorities had failed to collect the necessary documents from the doctor. He assured the minister that such negligence would not be repeated.
Talking to reporters after the drive, Sakhawat said the government spends substantial public funds to ensure healthcare services at government hospitals.
"If a government doctor neglects official duties to treat patients at a private facility, there will be no leniency," he said.
The minister warned that strict action would be taken against both government doctors and private healthcare institutions found involved in such irregularities.

item.title: City Corporation official dies after falling during warrant execution
item.description:
A Gazipur City Corporation accounts officer died after falling from the eighth floor of his apartment at Rangs Garden Palace on Siddheswari Road in Dhaka's Ramna area early Thursday.
The deceased was identified as Nazrul Islam, 55, who had an arrest warrant issued against him in a CR (complaint) case pending before a Gazipur court.
The incident took place at around 12:30am at the apartment building located at 63/B Siddheswari Road.
Confirming the incident, Ramna Police Station Sub-Inspector (SI) Md Uzzal said police had gone to the flat to execute the arrest warrant.
"Upon sensing the presence of police, Nazrul may have attempted to flee through the back door and taken shelter on the balcony ledge, or tried to move to a neighbouring flat. He apparently lost his footing during the attempt and fell from the building, sustaining critical injuries," the SI said.
He said Nazrul was rescued and taken to the emergency department of Dhaka Medical College Hospital (DMCH) at around 2:45am, where the on-duty physician declared him dead.

item.title: Govt tightens noise rules, bans night-time honking in residential areas
item.description:
The government has introduced tougher measures to curb noise pollution, including a ban on honking in residential areas between 9:00pm and 6:00am, as part of a new set of restrictions aimed at protecting public health and the environment.
The measures were announced in a public notice issued by the Department of Environment (DoE) on Thursday.
The DoE said noise pollution poses a serious threat to human health and biodiversity. To address the problem, the government has promulgated the Noise Pollution (Control) Rules, 2025, prescribing permissible noise limits for different areas and imposing stricter controls on noise-generating activities.
Under the rules, the maximum allowable noise level has been set at 40 decibels in silent zones and 75 decibels in industrial areas.
The rules also stipulate that:
(A)Noise generated by any equipment or activity must not exceed the prescribed limits.
(B) High-noise equipment may not be used in public places without prior written approval from the competent authority. Even with permission, the noise levelmust not exceed 90 decibels, operation is limited to five hours, and use must end before 11:00pm.
(C) The manufacture, import, storage, sale, display, distribution, marketing, transportation and use of horns exceeding the prescribed noise limits are prohibited.
(D) Honking is strictly prohibited in silent zones, where the use of firecrackers, fireworks and other noise-producing activities is also banned.
(E) Honking is prohibited in residential areas from 9:00pm to 6:00am.
(F)Picnics are banned in natural forests and wildlife habitats, and the use of loudspeakers or other high-noise equipment in such areas is prohibited.
(G)Construction machinery may not be operated between 7:00pm and 7:00am within 500 metres of the boundary of a residential area.
(H)Traffic sergeants or officers of higher rank are empowered to impose on-the-spot penalties for noise pollution offences committed in their presence.
The Department of Environment urged the public to comply with the new rules to help safeguard public health and protect the environment.
